A particle $P$ of mass $3\ \mathrm{kg}$ moves so that its position vector $\mathbf{r}$ at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$\mathbf{r} = [\,t(1-t)\,\mathbf{i} + t(\sin \pi t)\,\mathbf{j}\,]\ \mathrm{m}.$$

Find, when $t = 1$,

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Setting up.** $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are unit vectors along the fixed perpendicular axes, so the velocity is the derivative of the position vector with respect to $t$, using the product rule on each component:

$$\mathbf{v} = \frac{d\mathbf{r}}{dt} = (1 - 2t)\,\mathbf{i} + (\sin \pi t + \pi t\cos \pi t)\,\mathbf{j}\ \ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

At $t = 1$: $\sin\pi = 0$ and $\cos\pi = -1$, so

$$\mathbf{v}(1) = (1 - 2)\,\mathbf{i} + (0 + \pi\cdot 1\cdot(-1))\,\mathbf{j} = (-\mathbf{i} - \pi\,\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

**Momentum** is mass times velocity:

$$\mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v} = 3(-\mathbf{i} - \pi\mathbf{j}) = (-3\mathbf{i} - 3\pi\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$$

Its magnitude is $|\mathbf{p}| = 3\sqrt{1 + \pi^2} \approx 9.89\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$.

**Momentum at $t=1$: $\mathbf{p} = (-3\mathbf{i} - 3\pi\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$** (about $-3\mathbf{i} - 9.42\mathbf{j}$).

From part (a), $\mathbf{v}(1) = -\mathbf{i} - \pi\mathbf{j}$, so the speed squared is

$$v^2 = (-1)^2 + (-\pi)^2 = 1 + \pi^2$$

Kinetic energy:

$$E_k = \tfrac12 m v^2 = \tfrac12\times 3\times(1 + \pi^2) = \tfrac32(1 + \pi^2)\ \mathrm{J}$$

Numerically, $1 + \pi^2 = 10.8696$, so $E_k \approx 16.3\ \mathrm{J}$.

**Kinetic energy $= \tfrac32(1+\pi^2) \approx 16.3\ \mathrm{J}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown: the cosine of the angle between the velocity and the acceleration.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Acceleration.** Differentiate the velocity again (product rule on $\pi t\cos\pi t$):

$$\mathbf{a} = \frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = -2\,\mathbf{i} + \big(\pi\cos\pi t + \pi\cos\pi t - \pi^2 t\sin\pi t\big)\mathbf{j} = -2\,\mathbf{i} + \big(2\pi\cos\pi t - \pi^2 t\sin\pi t\big)\mathbf{j}$$

At $t = 1$:

$$\mathbf{a}(1) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + (2\pi(-1) - 0)\,\mathbf{j} = (-2\mathbf{i} - 2\pi\mathbf{j})\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$$

**Angle between $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{a}$.** Use $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{a}}{|\mathbf{v}||\mathbf{a}|}$ with $\mathbf{v} = -\mathbf{i} - \pi\mathbf{j}$:

$$\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{a} = (-1)(-2) + (-\pi)(-2\pi) = 2 + 2\pi^2$$

$$|\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{1 + \pi^2},\qquad |\mathbf{a}| = \sqrt{4 + 4\pi^2} = 2\sqrt{1 + \pi^2}$$

$$\cos\theta = \frac{2(1 + \pi^2)}{\sqrt{1 + \pi^2}\cdot 2\sqrt{1 + \pi^2}} = \frac{2(1+\pi^2)}{2(1+\pi^2)} = 1$$

**$\cos\theta = 1$.** This is because $\mathbf{a}(1) = 2\,\mathbf{v}(1)$: at $t=1$ the acceleration is parallel to the velocity and in the same direction ($\theta = 0$), so the particle is speeding up along its direction of motion.
